sections.body:
An airplane is a machine that carries people and cargo through the air. It has a long body, two big wings, a tail and some engines.

A plane is heavy. A big plane carries hundreds of people, and that weight is many tonnes. Yet it flies. How can something so heavy stay up in the air?

The answer is the **wing**. The shape of a wing is called an **airfoil**. When a plane moves forward, air flows over the top of the wing and around the bottom. The wing pushes some of that air down, and the air pushes back up on the wing. That upward push is called **lift**.

Lift is strong enough to hold up the whole plane. The wings are wide and long so there is lots of surface for the air to push against.

The engines do the pushing forward. The engines pull air backwards and push it away, and the plane moves forward. That is called **thrust**.

A plane keeps going because the wings keep making lift while the engines keep making thrust. It also has to fight the air that tries to slow it down. That slowing force is called **drag**.

And the whole time, the Earth pulls the plane down. That pull is called **gravity**. A good airplane is one where lift beats gravity, and thrust beats drag.
examples: An airplane is heavy, but its wings make enough lift to hold it up.
The engines push the plane forward.
The wings push air down, and the air pushes the wings up.
sections.heading: What an Airplane Is

sections.body:
Lift is the upward push that keeps an airplane in the air. It comes from the shape of the wing and from the speed of the plane.

Most airplane wings are curved on top and nearly flat underneath. They are called **wings with camber**. When the plane moves fast, air travels a little faster over the curved top than under the flat bottom. The air above moves more quickly, so it spreads out and presses down less. The air below presses down more. The difference in pressure pushes the wing up.

The wing also pushes some air downwards. Air that is pushed down has to go somewhere, and it swirls around behind the wing. This is the **downwash**, and it is another way the wing gets pushed up.

Speed matters a lot. Move the wing faster and the air presses harder, so the lift grows. That is why a plane must run fast along the ground before it can leave it.

The wings can change shape. On the ground, the flaps and the slats on the trailing edge fold down to make the wing bigger and clumsier. That helps the plane take off and land slowly. Once the plane is high, the wing tips fold up to save fuel.

Pilots also use small panels on the wings called **ailerons**. Moving them up or down rolls the plane to one side or the other, so the plane can turn.
examples: A wing with camber is curved on top and flat underneath.
The faster the plane goes, the more lift the wing makes.
The flaps fold down so the plane can land slowly.
sections.heading: How the Wings Make Lift

sections.body:
An airplane is made of parts that each do one job. Here are the ones you can point at on the ground.

The **fuselage** is the long tube that holds the passengers and the cargo. It is the body of the plane.

The **wings** are the wide flat parts on the sides. They make the lift.

The **engines** hang under the wings or sit at the back. They make the thrust. Some airplanes have jet engines and some have propeller engines, which spin blades like a fan.

The **tail**, called the empennage, is at the back. It has a vertical fin that keeps the plane pointing the right way, and horizontal stabilisers that keep the back of the plane steady.

The **landing gear** is the set of wheels. The wheels fold away after take-off, so they do not slow the plane down in the air.

The **cockpit** is at the front. This is where the pilots sit, and they steer the plane from there.

And the **control surfaces** are the small moving parts: the ailerons on the wings, the elevator on the tail and the rudder. The pilots move these to make the plane roll, pitch and turn.
examples: The fuselage is the long body that holds everyone.
The landing gear folds away after take-off.
The pilots sit in the cockpit at the front.
sections.heading: The Parts of an Airplane

sections.body:
Every flight follows the same path, and it is easy to follow along. The next time you go to an airport, watch for these steps.

First the plane is checked. People walk around it and look at the wheels, the wings and the engines. A fuel truck fills the tanks.

Then the passengers come on. They put their bags in the hold, and they find their seats. The pilots check the lists and talk to the control tower.

Then the doors close and the plane starts its engines. The engines make a loud humming sound.

Next the plane pushes back from the gate and taxi to the runway. Taxiing means rolling slowly on the ground.

Then comes the exciting part. The engines push the plane faster and faster. The wings make more and more lift. When the lift beats the weight, the wheels leave the ground. That is **take-off**.

In the climb, the plane tilts up and gains height. The crew turn on the seat belt sign.

At the other end, the plane slows down and the flaps come out. The landing gear comes down. The wheels touch the runway, and the plane slows down and rolls back to the gate.
examples: The engines are running, so the plane is getting ready to move.
Now the plane is taxiing to the runway.
The wheels are off the ground, so we have taken off.
sections.heading: What Happens Between the Gate and the Sky
steps: The ground crew check the plane and fill the fuel tanks.
Passengers put their bags away and take their seats.
The doors close and the engines start.
The plane pushes back from the gate and taxis to the runway.
The engines speed up until the wings lift the plane off the ground.
In the climb the plane tilts up and gains height.

sections.body:
These are the words you will hear about airplanes.

Lift is the upward push on the wings. It holds the plane up in the air.

Thrust is the forward push. The engines make it.

Drag is the air pushing back on the plane and trying to slow it down.

Gravity is the Earth's pull downwards. It tries to bring the plane down.

Airfoil is the shape of a wing. The curve on top and the flat part underneath are what make lift.

Flaps are moving panels on the back of the wing. They make the wing bigger for take-off and landing, so the plane can go slowly and stay in the air.

Take-off is the moment the wheels leave the ground. **Landing** is the moment they touch down again.
sections.heading: The Words We Use for Flying

terms.example: More speed means more lift on the wings.
terms.gloss: The upward push that the wings make on a plane. It is what holds the plane in the air.

terms.example: The engines give the plane its thrust.
terms.gloss: The forward push of a plane. The engines make the thrust.

terms.example: A smooth plane has less drag and uses less fuel.
terms.gloss: The force of the air pushing back against a plane and trying to slow it down.

terms.example: Lift has to be stronger than gravity to keep the plane up.
terms.gloss: The pull of the Earth that pulls everything downwards, including airplanes.

terms.example: A good airfoil makes lift with less speed.
terms.gloss: The shape of a wing. The curved top and flat bottom help the air push the wing up.

terms.example: The flaps come out so the plane can land slowly.
terms.gloss: Moving panels on the back edge of a wing. They make the wing bigger for take-off and landing.

sections.body:
Airports and planes are not places for playing. A plane engine can pull in a person from many metres away, even when the engine is quiet.

Never walk on the runway, and never walk on the grass near it. The grass is full of hidden lights and underground cables.

Never throw anything at a plane, even a small stone. A tiny object can damage an engine, and the plane must land somewhere unexpected.

Keep away from the fence near a runway. The noise of a plane is very loud, and it can damage your hearing.

And at home, remember that planes fly high and fast. Beaches, mountains and tall buildings are all far safer places to watch them than the airport fence. Watch them from a distance, and never try to get closer for a better photo.
sections.heading: Staying Safe Around Airports

item.summary: An airplane is heavy, and yet it flies. After reading this, you can explain why the wings hold a plane up, name the parts of an airplane, and tell what happens between the airport gate and the sky.
item.title: How Do Airplanes Fly?
